questions.prompt: Feeds are read about 20 times as often as posts are written. Why does that favour fan-out on write?

options.text: Writes are cheaper than reads in every database
Doing the merge work once per post, instead of on every feed open, makes the far more frequent reads cheap
Fan-out on write uses less storage

questions.explanation: Pay the cost on the rare operation (posting) to make the common one (reading) a single cache lookup.

questions.prompt: An account with 50 million followers posts. With pure fan-out on write and workers handling 300,000 inserts per second, roughly how long until every follower has it?

options.text: About 3 minutes, delaying other posts queued behind it

questions.explanation: 50,000,000 ÷ 300,000 ≈ 167 seconds. That's why huge accounts are excluded from fan-out and merged at read time instead.

questions.prompt: Why do timelines store post ids rather than full posts?

options.text: Edits and deletes don't require updating millions of timelines
Ids load faster than posts in every case
Posts can be cached once and shared by every timeline that references them

questions.explanation: Ids are 8 bytes and immutable; post content lives in one place, cached once, and changes there apply everywhere.

questions.prompt: Why use a cursor (the last post id seen) instead of page numbers for scrolling?

options.text: Page numbers are not allowed in REST APIs
New posts arriving at the top shift offset-based pages, causing duplicates or gaps; a cursor stays anchored

questions.explanation: "Posts older than id X" doesn't move when new posts arrive, so scrolling stays correct.

questions.prompt: 30% of users haven't opened the app in a month. What's a sensible way to handle them?

options.text: Keep fanning out to them so their feed is ready
Skip fan-out for them, and rebuild their timeline on demand with fan-out on read when they return

questions.explanation: Precomputing feeds nobody reads wastes inserts and memory. A one-time rebuild on return costs a little latency for a rare event.
